source: OECD (2025), Health at a Glance 2025: OECD Indicators, OECD Publishing, Paris
framing: Gap framing: every figure is what is NOT covered, NOT satisfied or unmet. Gap figures are 100 minus the published figure.
rule: HAL may phrase these facts freely but must not state any figure, ranking or claim that is not in this list. Verbatim report sentences may name other countries; only what they say about this country may be used.

facts.text: 59% of people in Hungary were NOT satisfied with the availability of quality healthcare where they live in 2024, versus an OECD average of 36%; satisfaction has deteriorated over the past decade.
26.3% of health spending in Hungary was NOT covered by government or compulsory insurance schemes in 2023, versus an OECD average of 24.9%.
1% of people in Hungary reported unmet medical care needs due to cost, distance or waiting times in 2024 (average of 28 OECD countries: 3.4%).
4% of hospital care costs in Hungary were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 11% on average in the OECD.
31% of outpatient medical care costs in Hungary were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 22% on average in the OECD.
61% of dental care costs in Hungary were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 68% on average in the OECD.
53% of pharmaceutical costs in Hungary were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 42% on average in the OECD.
Swiss citizens were most likely to be satisfied (89%), while those in Greece, Türkiye, Hungary, Italy, Chile and Colombia were least likely to be satisfied (lower than 50%).
More than 8% of people in Greece, Latvia and Iceland reported unmet dental care needs in 2024, compared to fewer than 1% in Germany, Hungary and the Netherlands, as well as accession country Croatia.

This varies considerably across OECD countries, from fewer than 2% of households experiencing catastrophic health spending in Sweden, Slovenia, the United Kingdom, Ireland and the Netherlands, to over 10% of households in Lithuania, Latvia and Hungary (Figure 5.10).
In terms of median number of days (Figure 5.11, right panel), this ranged from around 50 days or less in Spain, Poland, Hungary and Sweden, to 280 days in Slovenia.
In 2024, median waiting times ranged from 67 days in Sweden and Spain, to over half a year in Hungary (209 days), Chile (313 days), Poland (343 days), and almost two years in Slovenia (667 days).
Government transfers fund two-thirds of the social health insurance system in Chile, and over 50% of all their revenues in Hungary and Israel.
